evening.text:
The Lieutenant Colonel Vinay B who was famously known as “Birdie” in the Indian Army’s defunct Technical Support Division (TSD) has retired and has been praised by many.
“The last active officer serving in the unit, Lieutenant Colonel Vinay B has served our nation with distinction. Wishing him all the best. With his retirement, the TSD has come into limelight. TSD was formed in 2010 during the tenure of General V.K. Singh,” said in a tribute.
The formation of TSD came after concerns about Pakistan sponsored terrorism following the November 2008 Mumbai attacks. The TSD was formed to handle sensitive intelligence and covert activities targeting Lashkar-e-Taiba chief Hafiz Saeed.
It was part of the Directorate General of Military Intelligence and worked directly under the Army Chief. This was to help give the military the ability to combat threats using intelligence and covert operations. Previously it was reported that Lt Col Vinay B was one of the officers chosen by the commanding officer Colonel Hunny Bakshi. Birdie used to be part of the Research and Analysis Wing and was involved in operations targeting terrorist groups in Jammu and Kashmir and the Northeast.
As much of the work they do would be classified, it can be difficult to determine what specific missions they were carrying out. However, the TSD had some controversies around it. It was investigated by the Army after allegations about interception devices and secret service money. This led to the disbandment of the group in 2012 after General V.K. Singh retired.
There was a lot of media coverage and an investigation into how the TSD were operating.

evening.title: Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth
evening.text:
Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite.

The company's Suncatcher satellite, launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit, has responded to a ground station prompt to "Write a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the wonderful world spinning beneath you."

Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said that with Suncatcher's host and TPU trays powered up and machine learning tests completed, the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit.

"During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space," wrote Beals in a blog post.

And as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, the orbiting AI model responded over the downlink:

Blue marble below,

Data streams in silent grace,

Starlight feeds my core. ✨

Those roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 if generated through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs.

Add in a satellite weighing perhaps 500 kg, based on the mass of SpaceX's Starlink satellites, and a retail launch price of around $7,000 per kg, and you have a very expensive haiku.

According to Google's calculations, if the cost of getting a satellite into low Earth orbit can be brought down to $200/kg, the launch cost amortized over the satellite's useful life (~$810–7,500/kW/year) could be comparable to current electricity spending for terrestrial datacenters in the US (~$570–3,000/kW/year).

Google predicts that SpaceX could achieve that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance of that actually happening.

After the haiku, Beals said, "we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems." Next up: tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation.

Google has already done some laboratory testing of its Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server to see how well they can withstand a 67 MeV proton beam.

The system's high-bandwidth memory shows the most sensitivity in terms of the total ionizing dose – it exhibits irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), which is about 3× Google's minimum requirement for TID survival of 750 rad(Si).

"For typical transformer workloads, the observed SDC [silent data corruption] rate of approximately one event/17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of 1 per 3 million inferences, assuming 1 inference per second," Google researchers said in a paper published earlier this month.

"While this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of SEEs on training jobs, and the efficacy of system-level mitigations, requires further study."

Indeed, the study will continue. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another. ®

India’s Defence Export Boom: Windfall or Lasting Growth?
evening.text:
India saw defence exports hit an all-time high of Rs 38,424 crore in FY2025-26, but there is a clear divide between Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) and the private sector. Exports by DPSUs rose 151% while the private sector only rose 14% year-on-year.
Exports by DPSUs rose to Rs 21,071 crore versus Rs 17,353 crore by the private sector, compared to last year where DPSU exports were valued at Rs 8,389 crore and the private sector at Rs 15,233 crore, according to the Ministry of Defence.
This increase can be attributed to a high level of demand for ammunition and defence supplies across the globe, especially Europe due to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh has said that public sector exporters have seen benefits from countries increasing their armament supplies, however, he has also said that the current exceptional growth rates seen cannot be sustained.
According to trade data, India recorded around $816.8 million of exports relating to HS Chapter 93 items (arms, ammunitions parts etc) during calendar year 2025. This is a smaller category than the overall $38,424 crore figure quoted by the government, as it does not include aircraft, ships, electronics, components and other items.
While Indian ammunitions producers have seen increased demand from Europe for artillery shells, mortars, propellants etc., orders for ammunitions will not always be seen again at the same rate due to immediate stock requirements. India also exports radars, electronic warfare, patrol boats, helicopters, amongst other defence systems. India also supplies aerostructures and components to international aerospace.
While aircraft components produced in India for western companies are helping boost industrial exports, there is no real indication that India can export items like indigenous combat aircraft or warships.
While progress is being made in both areas, it is not clear how much of the Rs 38,424 crore figure can be attributed to original designs by India, components and items which have experienced temporary increases in demand. The government have published figures showing the overall export value and how it breaks down between public and private, but it would be good to see more detail.
It is difficult to compare customs data with the overall figure as it is not the same item categories. This does not mean that one of the figures is wrong.
The Department of Defence Production should provide more clarity on what the figure actually refers to and provide more detailed information to understand how much of the figure relates to actual exports, how much is from components and services and which items have had the most increase. There has been some focus on India’s ammunitions export as there have been reports of Indian-origin ammunitions being sent to Ukraine via European countries. India has denied that it has exported ammunitions directly to Ukraine, but Russia has raised concerns.
While India is still one of the largest importers of arms in the world, it is also increasing its production and exports. In the long term, it will be key that it moves past short-term increases in ammunitions demand and can secure repeat business internationally for more complex indigenous items. Over the next few financial years we will see if the DPSU increase leads to sustainable production, new clients and a broader portfolio of exports or if there will be a noticeable plateau in growth.

The LPA of rainfall over the country during the month of November, based on data from 1971 to 2020, is about 29.7 mm.South Peninsular India is also likely to experience 77 per cent of LPA during November. ENSO also has a neutral phase.Very strong El Nino conditions could be one of the key reasons why during this year's October, India witnessed the highest monthly average maximum temperature (32.43 degrees Celsius) since 1901. The normal monthly average maximum temperature for October is 31.37 degrees Celsius, according to the IMD.Moreover, the monthly average minimum temperature during this October was the fifth highest (20.83 degrees Celsius) since 1901. evening.title: HAL Seeks Environmental Testing Support as Fighter Production Scales Up
evening.text:
Although most headlines will focus on how many Tejas Mk1As HAL can deliver, how quickly Su-30MKIs can be upgraded or how many prototypes they can make for the AMCA, the truth of the matter may rest with just how rigorous their testing process is at the Tier-2 component level in the form of Environmental Stress Screening and Environmental Stress Testing.
Recent tenders at HAL for specialist environmental testing chambers at many of their manufacturing and overhaul facilities indicates that they are trying to streamline and increase their testing capabilities. A component can only be as good as the environmental chamber so if there is any issues at HAL or even at the MSMEs, this will cause delays in delivery.
The requirements for these tenders are much stricter than those seen in commercial and automotive industries. To meet standards of Military Airworthiness (MIL-STD-810) and JSS 55555, the environmental chambers need to be able to move temperature from the minimum to maximum at a rate of 10-20 Degrees Celsius per minute. This causes components to go through extreme temperature changes quickly, to ensure that any faults in manufacturing are found such as cracked solder joints or poor bonding on microchips. The temperature ranges need to go from -80 Degrees to +180 Degrees Celsius. This is because Indian Military aircraft can be expected to operate in extreme conditions from high altitude in the Himalayas to extreme heat on the tarmac. They also need to provide a temperature variance of +/- 1 Degrees Celsius across the various test drawers using high air flow and be able to remove the heat produced from electrical components whilst in operation. Typically this means they will have cascade cooling systems with semi-hermetic compressors and dry air purge systems.
Many MSMEs in the Private Sector will struggle to meet these requirements. Aerospace grade environmental testing chambers will cost a lot of money to purchase and will require complex PLC and HMI systems to monitor the data along with NABL certified sensors. Many smaller suppliers struggle with buying fully compliant chambers due to the cost. Many suppliers will have low grade or poorly calibrated thermal chambers.
The CEMILAC and DGAQA are responsible for flight worthiness and quality assurance in India and require full records of all environmental testing. This means that any components going into flight critical components such as flight computers, Radar Sub Assemblies or Actuation Hydraulics will need full records. If your Tier-2 supplier does not have monitoring of the thermal ramp rate, humidity control within a set range of 10-97% or combined vibration and thermal testing, then your entire batch will be rejected. This has nothing to do with the component itself but everything to do with the testing. To perform precise testing, they must be calibrated by a ISO/IEC 17025 accredited party. Many MSMEs outside of the major Aerospace manufacturing centres in India will struggle to meet the requirements of having the chambers calibrated. They will suffer downtime, refrigerants will have to be compliant with non CFC and HCFC requirements and will require an annual check. This will cause delays.
Overall it seems that HAL are looking to improve their environmental testing and standardise it across their facilities and suppliers. By improving compliance at Tier-2, it means that they can ensure quality assurance is done at an early stage rather than having to troubleshoot issues once they get to the flight line. In India, knowing how to meet the strict specifications required for environmental testing chambers are becoming increasingly important to meet their indigenous manufacturing goals.

evening.title: INS Vikrant’s Rafale M Milestone Gets a Close Look in China
evening.text:
The way that Chinese media has reported the Rafale Marine’s first landing on INS Vikrant has been centred on a point which got less emphasis in the initial Indian news reports namely, that the aircraft was piloted by a Dassault Aviation test pilot and that it was a test aircraft made by the manufacturer rather than one of the Rafale M fighters that India has ordered for its Navy.
The report which was issued by the Chinese news and comment site Guancha on October 30 and then reprinted by Sina stated that the Indian Navy had announced on October 29 the successful landing of a Rafale M on INS Vikrant. The report quoted Indian media, such as India Today, and regarded the event as an important milestone in the integration of the French fighter aircraft into India’s carrier operations.
The Chinese report also mentioned that India has still not received the 26 Rafale Marine aircraft which it ordered from France and stated that the aircraft used for the landing was a Dassault test aircraft with the number “1” on it rather than having the markings of an Indian Navy squadron.
The observation is factually relevant since the landing shows advances have been made in the certification of the aircraft for use on Indian carrier operations, even though it does not imply that the Navy has already received or operationally induced the aircraft. Guancha’s report was mainly descriptive, as it outlined the aircraft’s role and the technical differences between French and Indian carrier operations; highlighting the manufacturer’s test aircraft gives context to the milestone, but on its own this does not constitute an explicit rejection of India’s achievement.
The Global Times, which is supported by the Chinese government, has in the past adopted a more critical stance towards India’s aspirations regarding aircraft carriers and has maintained that the INS Vikrant is unable to compare with China’s more extensive carrier programme. It must, however, be noted that this general editorial position does not constitute a direct reply to this specific landing. The Rafale M was developed to operate from France’s Charles de Gaulle aircraft carrier, a ship that employs catapult-assisted take-off and arrested recovery, which is commonly referred to as CATOBAR.
The INS Vikrant and the INS Vikramaditya have a different arrangement: Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery, or STOBAR. Aircraft take off by means of a ski-jump ramp and land by using the arrestor wires on the flight deck.
The Rafale M’s successful landing on INS Vikrant thus represents an important step in verifying the aircraft for use by the Indian Navy on its carrier. However, further testing will still be needed before the type can be accepted for operational service with the Indian Navy.

evening.title: Exercise AUSTRAHIND: Indian and Australian Troops Demonstrate Joint Capabilities
evening.text:
In a step towards deepening India-Australia defence cooperation, the military of both countries showcased enhanced interoperability and joint operational capabilities during a joint Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) training in coastal terrain as part of Exercise AUSTRAHIND 2026 in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala.
During the exercise, the Indian Navy’s INS Sharda and a Sea King helicopter, in coordination with the Indian and Australian armies, carried out a swift ship-to-shore troop insertion, demonstrating the seamless integration of land, sea and air capabilities.
Sharing the details in a post on X on Saturday, the Indian Navy’s Southern Naval Command said, “During AUSTRAHIND2026 at Thiruvananthapuram, Indian Navy’s INS Sharda and Sea King helicopter, in close coordination with the Indian Army and Australian Army, executed a swift ship-to-shore troop insertion as part of joint HADR training in coastal terrain.”
“The exercise showcased seamless integration of land, sea and air capabilities, reinforcing jointmanship, interoperability and operational readiness while strengthening India-Australia defence cooperation,” it added.
Underscoring the broader significance of the bilateral exercise, Australian High Commissioner to India, Philip Green, took to X and posted, “I had the privilege of seeing Australia-India troops training side by side at Ex AUSTRAHIND 2026. Bilateral exercises like these strengthen mutual understanding & interoperability, build trust and deepen our defence partnership.”
The 5th edition of the India-Australia Joint Military Exercise AUSTRAHIND 2026 commenced on October 19 at the Foreign Training Node, Thiruvananthapuram, with a focus on coordinated operations in coastal and island environments, surveillance and reconnaissance, said the Ministry of Defence.
The exercise, which will run until November 1, witnessed the participation of approximately 120 personnel each from the Indian Army and the Australian Army.
Earlier this week, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh held a meeting with Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles on the sidelines of the 13th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in the Philippines to review defence cooperation, boost military interoperability, and address regional security challenges.
Singh emphasised the importance India places on its Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with Australia for a free, open, and secure Indo-Pacific.
“Delighted to meet Australia’s Deputy PM and Defence Minister, Mr. Richard Marles, on the sidelines of the ADMM-Plus meeting today. We had productive discussions on reviewing our bilateral defence cooperation, enhancing military interoperability, and addressing regional security challenges. India places great value on its Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with Australia for a free, open, and secure Indo-Pacific,” Singh posted on X.

Focusing first on the target-drone function would enable air-defence units to carry out exercises in which they practise detecting, tracking and engaging fast-moving aerial threats. Using such targets would allow crews to assess the performance of their radar, the engagement procedures and the way in which sensors and weapon systems co-ordinate. Apollyon has proposed a multi-role strategy for the Nightshade platform, with versions designed for use as an aerial target, for decoy operations and for the loitering-munition role.
The model intended for training purposes would be used for that specific purpose, while the version oriented towards strike missions would constitute a separate application that would need its own development and evaluation. The figure of 15 kg for the payload also has to be understood in light of the various configurations of the platform. A aircraft used for training would carry the equipment suitable to its role and would not have to use the same payload as a strike version.
Today’s air-defence crews have to deal with an increasing variety of aerial threats, ranging from small unmanned aircraft and loitering munitions to faster cruise-missile-type targets. It is important to train using realistic targets, but the extent to which any given drone can simulate a particular threat will depend on its speed, flight path, radar signature and manoeuvrability. The 700 km/h performance that has been stated could mean that the Nightshade becomes relevant to exercises involving faster aerial targets. Nevertheless, its suitability for use in S-400 training will have to be determined by military assessment, the characteristics of the target and the training needs of the units involved.
The stated 300 km range does not in itself show how far the drone can operate from a ground-control station or under specific mission conditions. The Nightshade Mk-2 shows a wider trend among Indian startups to go beyond conventional multirotor drones and move towards jet-powered systems with more specific defence uses. If its performance and reliability are confirmed, the target-drone configuration could provide the armed forces with another indigenous choice for air-defence training.

evening.title: Goth aesthetic gone wild: a user's self-inflicted black screen of non-death in Windows 3.1’s
evening.text:
Microsoft senior software engineer Raymond Chen has explained what Windows is doing when you hold down the power button, and shared a story about the time a customer accidentally created a Goth Mode for Windows 3.1.

There's a section in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (actually, page 116 of this writer's dog-eared copy of The Restaurant at the End of the Universe) in which Zaphod Beeblebrox observes of a ship's interior: "Every time you operate one of these weird black controls that are labeled in black on black background, a little black light lights up black to let you know you've done it."

The same turned out to be true of a user who called Microsoft customer support to complain that after Windows 3.1 booted up, all that remained after the product logo disappeared was a blank screen.

It turned out the customer liked black a little too much and, according to Chen, made themself a Goth theme.

The customer support engineer on Microsoft's end pieced it together. The customer had, according to Chen, "set the wallpaper color to black. They set the title bar color to black. They set the button color to black. They set the window background color to black. They set the window text color to black.

"Every possible color you could pick in the Colors control panel was set to black."

We suspect the mouse pointer, at least, would have stuck around, unless the customer had also managed to change some settings around this. And then there are the icons… However, Windows 3.1 was a long time ago, and this writer's attempts at theming then were the consequences of growing up in the '70s and '80s, which resulted in some interesting neon, orange, and brown combinations.

As for Goth mode, Chen said, "Once you get yourself into this situation, it’s hard to get out because you can't see anything." One solution he suggested was deleting the [colors] section from the win.ini file.

Chen told the anecdote as a coda to the question – what exactly is modern Windows doing when you hold down the power button on a PC? According to Chen, after eight seconds of holding the power button, the Windows kernel realizes a forced power-off is happening and tries to take a kernel dump for diagnostics.

He explained that the kernel dumps were classified by Microsoft as "long power button hold" (LPBH) failures, with one of the bits of information captured indicating if all the pixels on the screen were black. The video driver might therefore be the culprit. Or whatever was responsible for drawing to the screen.

Today's Windows struggles with dark mode. But in the dim, distant past, every pixel being black might mean the user was either Hotblack Desiato or had done something very silly indeed. ®

evening.text:
The Indian Air Force (IAF) has put out a new tender for upgrading/replacing three avionics items used in their fleet of Mi-17 series helicopters to reduce foreign dependence. The tender, posted on 22 October 2026, seeks to procure a Primary Information Sensor Unit (PISU), search and landing light, with gyro horizon for the Mi-17V5T helicopter. The Directorate of Engineering (D) within the Indian Air Force is handling the process using a two bid process. Bids have to be submitted by 11am on 17th December 2026. EMD has been set at ₹5 crore and the duration of the project is 730 days.
The reason for the procurement of these three items is interesting as they were included in an IAF procurement in 2024. Although there is no indication as to why this procurement hasn’t been completed, it would be premature to assume the last procurement didn’t go ahead due to a lack of compliant bids.
When upgrading avionics it is more complex than finding a component with similar specs. The replacement item needs to function reliably and also integrate safely into the aircraft. Developing test equipment, diagnostic tools and evidence for certifying can become large portions of the project if there isn’t much design information from the manufacturer.
The IAF have acknowledged these issues. Air Marshal Vijay Kumar Garg, the current Air Officer Commanding-in-Chief for Maintenance Command, spoke about the difficulty of dealing with avionics without design information during AVISEM-25, a 2 day seminar about developing avionics and product lifecycle management. He called for indigenous diagnostic tools, test equipment and increased cooperation between the IAF, DRDO, certifying bodies and industry.
This procurement for the Mi-17 is part of an effort to increase indigenous capabilities for maintaining aircraft that may no longer have timely or comprehensive support from the manufacturer. There is no indication from the tender notice as to whether these items will be completely redesigned, upgraded using existing designs, or a combination of both. The location of the project can be found as 3 BRD Chandigarh from the official e-procurement site.
The pre-bid meeting will take place at 9 BRD Pune on 25th November 2026. This shows the tenders are linked to both locations, however there is no indication the project will take place in Pune. This procurement is part of an overall effort by the IAF to increase indigenous capabilities. In July 2026, the IAF published a list of requirements titled Sankalp-2026 in conjunction with the Society of Indian Defence Manufacturers. This was an effort to encourage Indian industry to develop equipment and spares for military aircraft.

evening.title: Amazon sends chills through its workforce with mixed message memo about AI use
evening.text:
There's a ridiculously simple test you can use to figure out whether AI mandates at a given company are well-considered, or are being shoved out the door by out-of-touch buffoons: What happens when an engineer documents that AI made a task worse? Are they taken seriously, or are they marginalized and eventually managed out?

Conveniently, this week Amazon published a treatise by Terk Terkowitz, a VP/Distinguished Engineer/Final Boss of Their Independent Contributor Technical Career Track, on the role of the developer in the age of AI. It was originally an internal missive sent to their software engineers and their managers back in September, which is an interesting lag for a document that sounds this confident. It also maps exceedingly well to what other organizations are struggling with.

I think it's a good document, but I can't help but view it with a somewhat cynical eye. I see it as an attempt to make the future of the profession of software engineering feel less bleak. And it's feeling mighty bleak for a lot of folks right now.

What's the context?

This treatise comes at a time of dramatic upheaval. Tech as an industry is no stranger to change (usually at 3AM, heralded by the pager), but something about the current AI-ification of the world strikes many of us as fundamentally dissimilar from previous revolutions. Folks are scared about their career prospects. "Should I give up tech and get into farming?" is a sincere question multiple people have asked me. I don't know! Tech is already a goat rodeo, so you've got a leg up if you do?

This anxiety isn't theoretical. In May, Amazon wisely shut down KiroRank, an employee-built cash incineration leaderboard that ranked people by token usage, after the obvious thing happened: people spun up junk tasks to climb the ranks. This is now called "tokenmaxxing," and the Terkowitz treatise specifically calls it out as being at odds with "frugality." Meta did the same thing with "Claudenomics" and 85K employees that same week. And Amazon reportedly announced another 250 job cuts this week. I can't tell you that these things are related. But I can tell you that every engineer who read the memo assumes that they are.

What's the thing say?

This document contains a lot of great stuff. I have a tremendous level of respect, both personal and professional, for Amazon's Principal Engineering community; I'm led to understand that that respect may not be reciprocated, but that's okay. I am, by their standards, a lapsed engineer who ran away to join the circus as one of its lesser clowns.

Terkowitz's memo emphasizes customer outcomes and engineering judgement, two things I would absolutely not delegate to AI any time soon. (Note: I am writing this in October of 2026, with the full understanding that previous comments on the capabilities where AI falls short tend to age like fine milk.) It documents work that (today) AI tools aren't improving. That's way better than assuming that every objection to AI inherently comes from some self-interested Luddite who's scared of being replaced. It also says something smart about measurement: look at the 90th percentile of AI adoption, at those teams burning the most tokens, and check whether their delivery actually went up commensurately. This is great! Shout it from the rooftops; we should all be doing such things.

But still, I wonder.

The memo says “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing.” Document it, bring it to your manager, work through the problem. I agree with every word of that! The question is whether anyone's promo doc is gonna survive citing it.

Here's what happens next. The memo concedes that input metrics are "deeply flawed," but then in the next paragraph says to go ahead and use them anyway, carefully. It then warns that non-adopters are falling behind. Those are three different positions within three sentences and they're not at all aligned with one another.

That's not muddled; I think it's cover. A manager can cite "a finding, not a failing" when a strong engineer skips the AI tool, and then cite "falling behind" when it's time to PIP someone. Both are congruent with their stated policy; you get to decide which interpretation you want to go with in a given situation.

How will managers handle justified AI non-use? Are promotion and performance decisions being made in a way that rewards these long term outcomes? Or are they instead taking the easy weasel way out, optimizing for what's cheap to measure, and rewarding tool activity? Because if you give me a metric, I will turn it into a target. So will an overwhelming majority of employees. When that happens, everyone loses — it's how KiroRank happened in the first place.

Everyone's selling tokens — including Amazon

I write this after two days of attending GitHub Universe, where they talked about how agents start roughly 40% of PRs now. And yet, Jay Parikh’s keynote argument was that useful output wasn't "more code," but rather completed outcomes: features shipped, bugs fixed, security issues addressed, loudmouth columnists silenced, etc. The problem here is that their entire business model cuts against that; they're billing in a model that charges customers on a consumption basis, not an output basis. There's nothing, today, that ties "AI spend" to "output that was worth the effort."

Which brings us back to Amazon. The memo says tokenmaxxing is at odds with frugality, and for Amazon’s internal cost line, it is. Meanwhile AWS bills Bedrock and Kiro customers by the token. Inside the building, tokenmaxxing is a problem to be stamped out. Outside it, it’s the revenue plan. ®

AW101, S-92 or H225M: India’s VVIP Helicopter Choice
evening.text:
India has approved the procurement of 24 Special Utility Helicopters for the Indian Air Force, with a reported cost of around ₹10,000 crore. This has brought back into focus what type of helicopter would be best to transport the President, Vice-President and Prime Minister. The new helicopters provide a modern upgrade from the current Mi-17 V5 helicopters and will have state-of-the-art self-protection systems to protect against attacks from the ground.
The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) gave the Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) on the 26 th October 2026. Media reports suggest that the Airbus H225M (or H-725) and Sikorsky S-92 could be among the shortlisted candidates. The Government have not officially confirmed any shortlist but it has been reported that direct imports could be considered due to the low quantity required.
The Leonardo AW101 provides a three engine option. This design allows increased flexibility in the event of an engine failure. The large cabin has dedicated areas for VVIP, crew and support, along with secure transportation areas.
Having three engines gives an added level of safety in challenging takeoff and flying over difficult terrain. However, there are many factors to consider. The helicopters need to offer high altitude performance, single engine capability, self-protection, secure cabin and all weather capability.
The S-92 offers an added advantage, with the VH-92A variant providing the US presidential lift capability. The H225M provides a twin engine option, with a large cabin and optional long range and self-protection capabilities. Ultimately it will come down to what configurations are provided for India.
In the past, India had chosen to procure the AW101 for their VVIP helicopter requirement. In February 2010 a deal was signed for 12 helicopters, valued at around ₹3,727 crore. According to the Indian Governments evaluation, the AW101 satisfied the qualitative requirements of the service. The Sikorsky S-92 however did not meet the requirement in four areas; missile approach warning, service ceiling, drift-down altitude and out of ground effect hover.
Unfortunately this did not go ahead. The deal was cancelled from 1 st January 2014 due to breaches of the pre-contract integrity agreement and breach of contract. The cancellation came after allegations of corruption and became one of the most politically sensitive deals in India.
This means any suggestion of the AW101 being chosen again will be politically challenging. It also shows how important a transparent evaluation will be and having clear service requirements. The self-protection capabilities will be very important for the new helicopters. Systems such as missile warning, radar, laser warning receiver, countermeasures, secure communications and armour will all be key in ensuring the helicopters can perform in a high threat environment.
The indicative price for 24 helicopters is around ₹417 crore each. This is based on an overall price of ₹10,000 crore. The price could include self-protection systems, VVIP interiors, communications, training, spares and long term support.

evening.text:
Today's bit of signage silage is either Windows 10 protesting that it is not part of London's Oxford Street pedestrianization, or someone failing to heed an alert before the public is made all too aware that things aren't going well…

Eagle-eyed Register reader Aaron Colwill spotted the sign outside the food hall entrance of a Marks & Spencer store on London's Oxford Street. It usually entices passersby through the doors with promises of treats inside, but today it appears to require a different kind of feeding. Disk space is running low.

Marks and Spencer (also known as M&S and Marks and Sparks) is no stranger to cyber whoopsies, having been the victim of an attack in 2025 in which crooks made off with customer data. Later that year, it reckoned cleanup costs would be about £136 million.

Colwill reckoned that Windows 10 21H2 LTSC was behind the problems. It could well be. While support for 21H2 ended for many users in 2023, Windows 10 LTSC 2021 will carry on until Jan 12, 2027, meaning engineers might have an exciting festive period ahead of them. Windows 10 IoT Enterprise LTSC 2021 will receive extended support until Jan 13, 2032.

Either way, using Windows to advertise the Food Hall's wares seems slightly overkill. Simple posters, for example, never run out of disk space or attract the bork fairy's attention.

Perhaps they might use something that lacks the voracious appetite for storage that Microsoft's finest demands. According to the Windows biz, installing Windows 10 requires at least 32 GB of disk space, ideally more. It all seems a bit excessive for a cake-based caterpillar advert. Then again, when your operating system tends to have the resilience of a chocolate teapot, using it to advertise a chocolate insect might not be such a bad idea after all. ®

evening.title: Backbone of a beast – charting Nvidia's rise to networking titan
evening.text:
Nvidia is more than just a leader in graphics and AI hardware. It has also become a titan of the networking industry with bigger datacenter Ethernet sales than any other vendor.

In Q2, Nvidia's networking revenues topped $17.5 billion. To put that in perspective, Cisco's revenue during that same period, across all products, was $17.3 billion.

GPUzilla's arrival as a networking power feels sudden, yet Jensen Huang started working towards this status in 2019 with the $6.9 billion acquisition of long-time networking partner Mellanox .

At the time, Mellanox wasn't a big name in Ethernet switching. The company was mostly known for its ConnectX NICs and InfiniBand switches. Outside of high-performance computing (HPC) and supercomputing clusters, and a big deployment at Microsoft, InfiniBand wasn't widely deployed in hyperscale datacenters.

Buying Mellanox allowed Nvidia to reposition itself as a system builder, which means something different in the context of distributed compute. Nvidia understood its datacenter customers weren't interested in buying GPUs or even servers; they wanted clusters of systems. For that, Nvidia needed interconnect and Mellanox's InfiniBand fit the bill.

Relentless co-design

Over the years, Huang has talked about co-design – designing components and software to work together for specific set of jobs rather than to be the best GPU, switch, or NIC. Its work with Mellanox is a prime example of that approach.

According to Dell'Oro Group analyst Sameh Boujelbene, Nvidia's decision to integrate compute and networking became key to the company's success.

"Customers choose Nvidia for its tightly integrated compute and networking architecture, optimized for AI workloads," she told The Register. That integration makes deployments easier and speeds time to market.

Ben Mabey, CTO of pioneering AI and machine learning company Recursion, told The Reg Nvidia's integration schemes won him over.

Founded in 2013, nearly a decade before ChatGPT made AI the subject of dinner-table discussion, Recursion sought to apply machine learning running atop GPUs to the problem of drug discovery.

This work involved churning through massive datasets which, Mabey tells us, now total more than 50 petabytes in size.

"When you think about our workloads, it makes LLMs workload training seem easy compared to the amount of data that has to be moved around," he told The Register.

"In the biological space and sciences in general, it's not well appreciated just how big the data actually is," he added. "The internet's big, but in the grand scheme of things, the text that people are training on is actually pretty small, versus the petabytes of data that we have of these images."

Recursion's first cluster was a system called BioHive Zero which it cobbled together from GTX 1080 graphics cards originally intended for gaming systems. It used Ethernet to connect GPUs and ran into the limits of conventional networking.

So, for its second cluster, an A100-based machine with around 300 accelerators, Recursion went with Nvidia's Quantum InfiniBand switches and ConnectX NICs.

As Mabey explains it, buying its compute and interconnects from the same vendor vastly simplified optimization and troubleshooting. When Recursion reached out to Nvidia for help tuning the system, they were able to consider it as a single system, rather than discrete compute and networking resources. This level of integration had only previously been offered by boutique supercomputer builders like Cray or Atos (Eviden/Bull/whatever it gets renamed next).

A wider Spectrum

Nvidia hasn't always listed networking revenue as a single line item in its financials. However, based on CFO commentary and a little back of the napkin math we can fill in the blanks.

Nvidia's networking revenues have grown steadily since the Mellanox acquisition. At two moments, its revenue shot up suddenly.

The first came in the 2023 calendar year (FY24) after OpenAI kicked off the AI gold rush with the launch of ChatGPT.

The second spread across 2024 and 2025, when Nvidia started selling Blackwell-generation GPUs and then started to ship them in large quantities.

"I see two major inflection points, both coinciding with the Blackwell platform ramp: the introduction of NVLink switches and the accelerating adoption of Spectrum-X Ethernet switches for AI back-end networks, driven by growing deployments of Nvidia GPU clusters and increased attach rates of Nvidia switches, NICs, optics, and cables," Boujelbene said.

It was around this time that users started deploy to Ethernet switches in large volume across Nvidia clusters. Elon Musk's Colossus supercomputer was one of the earliest examples.

As we reported at the time, the first half of the 200,000-chip H100 and H200-based cluster came online in 2024 and, at the time, was among the largest ever clusters deployed using Nvidia's Spectrum-X Ethernet switches.

Meta has also made extensive use of Nvidia's Spectrum switches in its own training clusters, including at its million-GPU Prometheus site in New Albany, Ohio.

There are a couple reasons Nvidia's Spectrum-X offering is doing so well.

First, through a combination of Spectrum Ethernet switches, superNICs, and some clever software optimizations, Nvidia was able to replicate many of the qualities that made InfiniBand so attractive while also benefiting from significantly higher radix and interoperability.

Ethernet switches, including Nvidia's own, have historically offered more ports. The higher the radix, the fewer switches are necessary to support a cluster at a given port speed.

This often gets misconstrued to mean that InfiniBand can't scale beyond clusters of a certain size, which isn't necessarily the case. But for clusters exceeding a certain number of GPUs, Ethernet is often more economical because it requires less equipment while achieving similar utilization.

That said, Nvidia's Spectrum-X isn't exactly unique. Broadcom, Cisco, AMD and others have managed to achieve utilization similar to InfiniBand through various investments in smartNICs and switches.

Nvidia's main differentiator, as Mabey and Boujelbene noted earlier, is the level of integration between the compute and networking.

The next frontier

Then Blackwell hit the market, enabling much greater scale and creating a surge in Nvidia's networking revenue.

Prior to Blackwell, Nvidia's NVLink and NVSwitch interconnect tech had largely been limited to single systems with up to eight GPUs. With the launch of the GB200 NVL72, these NVSwitches were broken out into dedicated appliances. (And yes, we remember GH200 NVL256 and NVL32, but from what we can tell these were never shipped in any meaningful volume, if at all.)

For every NVL72 rack system sold, Nvidia also sold nine NVSwitch trays, which enabled the system's six dozen GPUs to function as a single enormous GPU. This effectively guaranteed steady networking revenue growth: even if customers didn't buy Nvidia's scale-out switches, if they wanted NVL72 racks, they were automatically buying NVSwitch.

"We estimate that NVSwitch now accounts for roughly one-third of Nvidia’s networking revenue, up from virtually zero less than two years ago," Boujelbene told El Reg. "This underscores how quickly NVLink switching has become a major growth engine for Nvidia’s networking business."

Nvidia is now moving to grow its networking business even further with a new licensing program.

Until recently, Nvidia's NVSwitch tech was limited to its own accelerators. However, with the introduction of NVLink Fusion early last year, Nvidia opened the interconnect tech up to third parties to license.

Many chip designers, including Marvell, Qualcomm, Arm, Fujitsu, MediaTek, and d-Matrix, have announced plans to develop CPUs and XPUs using NVLink Fusion. The adoption of the interconnect opens the door to additional NVSwitch sales, as the chips using NVLink Fusion still rely on them for chip-to-chip communications, and there's no other place to get them, as Nvidia has yet to license out NVSwitch.

"NVLink Fusion allows Nvidia to extend its networking footprint beyond its own GPUs into the rapidly growing custom accelerator market. I see it as a strategic move to capture a larger share of AI networking spending, even in clusters that do not use Nvidia GPUs," Boujelbene said.

Nvidia's networking ambitions don't stop there.

"Nvidia continues to pursue opportunities in emerging networking domains as network requirements evolve to keep pace with increasingly demanding AI workloads," Boujelbene added. "The latest example is scale-in networking, designed to address the new requirements of agentic AI, while innovations such as CPO will help overcome growing bandwidth, power, and scalability challenges." ®
